content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the problem of continuous unsupervised domain adaptation, which is a combination of continual learning and domain adaptation. The goal is to learn a model such that it can retain high accuracy in previously seen domains while still being able to effectively adapt to current/future domains. The authors argue that the two extremes, Bobu et al. (2018) and Tang et al. (2021), do not work perfectly and therefore propose to train two separate encoders, each of which corresponds to the two terms in Bobu et al. (2018).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 

+ The problem of continuous domain adaptation is certainly interesting and important. 

Weaknesses

- The organization of the paper could be improved. 

- Notation could be improved. There are a lot of places where notation is used without prior definition. 

- The paper is not very well written, especially the method section. The authors seem to overly rely on plain-text description, without rigorous mathematical abstraction. This makes the method section extremely vague and makes it very difficult for readers to fully understand the technical details of the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The organization of the paper could be improved. Given the 2-page-long introduction, it would be a better idea to move some of the introduction into the related work section. It is also a bit atypical to put the related work section as the third section after the method section. 

In terms of literature review, the paper seems to build heavily on Bobu et al. (2018) and therefore devoted a lot of space to introducing this prior method, but it misses a lot of more recent work on continuous domain adaptation, e.g., [1] and [2]. 

Notation could be improved. There are a lot of places where notation is used without prior definition. For example, what is $x_0$ and $x_T^t$. Does $x_0$ refer to one of the data point in the source domain? If so, how do you denote other data points in $D_0$. Does the subscript $T$ mean ‘target domain’ or refer to the T-th domain. Since you are referring to the current domain, why is it $D_0$ rather than $D_{t-1}$? Do you assume there is only one source domain, or do you assume a continual DA setting. If it is the latter, using $D_{t-1}$ would be more appropriate? If you denote $D_0$ as a data distribution, it should be $D_0(x)$. 

The equations are written in a rather informal way and are therefore by no means rigorous. It would be helpful if the paper could be significantly revised by someone with more rigorous math training before submission. In Eq (4), it is also strange and misleading to use $w$ to denote gradient; perhaps $g_w$ is better. 

The description of the F2L method is very confusing, with multiple typos. Along with the confusing and undefined notation, this makes it very difficult to understand what is actually proposed beyond the very high level idea of training two encoders, one to remember previous domains and one to adapt for future/current domains. 

What is the difference between $\hat{E}$ and $E$?


I feel that essentially training two separate encoders does not fundamentally solve the dilemma of remembering previous domains and adapting to current domains. At the end of the day, this is somehow equivalent to simply doubling the model capacity such that one has a larger model to do both. 

Another one of my major concerns is the very limited experiment results. For example, in Table 1, the only actual baseline is Bobu et al. (2018), which is a simple baseline from 4 years ago. Again, the paper is missing a lot of highly relevant recent works as baselines [1, 2]. 

The authors only evaluated their method on two datasets, i.e., rotating MNIST and 5 Digits. Both are very simple datasets. Along with the missing baselines, it is therefore insufficient to draw any meaningful conclusions on whether the proposed method is making any improvements upon the state of the art. 


[1] Gradient regularized contrastive learning for continual domain adaptation. AAAI 2021. 

[2] Continuously indexed domain adaptation. ICML 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper tackles the problem of continuous unsupervised domain adaptation, which is a combination of continual learning and domain adaptation. The proposed method heavily builds upon Bobu et al. (2018), essentially with the idea to train two separate encoders, each of which corresponds to the two terms in Bobu et al. (2018). My main concerns for the paper include (1) the absence of highly relevant and recent baselines, (2) limited technical merit, compared to Bobu et al. (2018), (3) presentation and organization that could be improved, especially in terms of mathematical rigor and clarity, (4) limited empirical results (only two synthetic datasets). Therefore I believe this submission is clearly below the bar for ICLR this year.

content.title: Reviewer 3-3
content.comment:
**Reviewer Comment:** 

*"I feel that essentially training two separate encoders does not fundamentally solve the dilemma of remembering previous domains and adapting to current domains. At the end of the day, this is somehow equivalent to simply doubling the model capacity such that one has a larger model to do both. "*

**Response:** 
* We would like to draw the reviewer's attention to the fact that only the generalist is needed during inference. Accordingly, the parameters learned for the specialist are not contributing by any means during inference. The specialist is only needed to train the generalist and is not used during the inference phase. Even during training, these trained parameters can be utilized sequentially, not simultaneously, where the new parameters delete the older ones. Thus what matters is the total number of training times rather than the total number of parameters. 
* Although F2L involves training two encoders, it does not increase but even reduces computational requirements. In total, (Generalist and Specialist) F2L needed 72% fewer epochs to converge than Bobu. This faster convergence is due to the simpler, non-conflicting, single objective function used for each stage of F2L. Also, it is critical to note that when training the specialist in the F2L approach (i.e., which takes the majority of the time, 76%), only the source and target domain data are needed, not the stored data in the memory buffer. This means that the data in the memory buffer is processed only when training the generalist, which is only 24% of the F2L total training time. While for Bobu to be able to calculate the multi-task loss term, the data from the memory buffer are processed 100% of the time. This shows that F2L needs a less total number of epochs and the less total number of FLOPS. 
* Although we showed that our proposed approach in its original form is at least computationally and memory equivalent to using a single encoder due to its simpler loss function, we run the following experiment to convince the reviewer further. We trained a modified encoder architecture for both the generalist and specialist with only half the number of filters in the original LeNet-5 architecture. This effectively makes the total number of learned parameters the same. The table below still shows that F2L maintains its superiority even when a smaller architecture is used.
| Method | ADiA | APA | AHA | ALA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobu: lambda= 0.10 | -0.13 | 0.94 | 0.84 | 0.81 |
| Specialist | -0.54 | 0.96 | 0.38 | 0.41 |
| Generalist | -0.02 | 0.95 | 0.93 | 0.93 |
| Smaller Specialist | -0.58 | 0.94 | 0.34 | 0.36 |
| Smaller Generalist | -0.04 | 0.94 | 0.91 | 0.90 |

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors tackle the problem of continual unsupervised domain adaptation (CUDA), where the training data arrives sequentially without labels except the labeled source data. To address the well-known stability-plasticity dilemma, they propose to train two models: one model is a specialist the other model is a generalist. The specialist learns the unsupervised target data by the conventional adversarial domain adaptation methods such as gradient reversal or ADDA. The generalist learns to not forget the previous data by minimizing the distillation loss with the exemplar and the corresponding pseudo-labels stored in a replay memory. They validate the proposed method on public benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper has the following strengths.

S1. The problem they tackle, continual unsupervised domain adaptation, is an important yet under-explored problem. In practice, we do not know all the domains of interest in advance. Furthermore, annotating every domain of interest is expensive. Therefore, CUDA is an interesting, and important problem to address.

S2. The proposed method shows a good stability-plasticity trade-off as shown in Fig. 2 and 3, Tables 1 and 2.

However, this paper has a few weaknesses as well.

W1. The proposed method uses two models which means there are twice the learnable parameters compared to the existing methods. Therefore, the comparisons with existing methods are unfair. To be fair, compared methods should learn the same amount of parameters. That means the compared method could expand the model along the way of continual learning. To justify the proposed method, there should be a baseline that expands learned parameters during each continual learning step, and finally, the total number of learned parameters is the same as the number of learned parameters of the proposed method. For now, we do not know if the good trade-off shown in the results is due to more parameters or due to the specialist-generalist learning paradigm.

W2. Unsupported claims. There are many unsupported claims in the paper. They should be supported by either citation, empirical results, or proof. To list a few:

C1) “Since the Generalist model is trained with pseudo-labeled samples from all previous domains, stability is no longer an issue.” -> Stability still might be an issue.

C2) “However, since the pseudo labels in the current approach are generated from the domain-specialist model (i.e., the high plasticity encoder), the quality of pseudo is expected to be at its highest. ” -> The quality of the pseudo-label still could be an issue. If the domain gaps are significant, the effect of noisy pseudo-label could be even detrimental.

C3) “This is because the fundamental reason why the multi-task approach does not work is that the two tasks are conflicting in nature, not because the replay loss is not effective enough to guarantee knowledge retention, as proposed by Tang et al. (2021).”

C4) “For example, in Figure 3, increasing λ from 0.01 to 0.1 can be justified, but from 0.1 to 1 is not.” -> Why this is the case? How to determine which increase can be justified?

W3. Presentation quality should be significantly improved. The introduction section is written more like a related work section. There are many errors, inconsistencies, awkward/wrong sentences, and typos throughout the paper. To list a few below:

- “Bobu et al. (2018), inspired by rehearsal methods Yoon et al. (2021) in continuous learning, proposed extending Wulfmeier et al. (2018) by utilizing an extra loss term denoted the replay loss.” -> awkward

- “Although the multi-task approach proposed Bobu et al. (2018) and its derivatives can effectively reduce catastrophic forgetting … ” -> awkward

- “This is especially critical as a result of machine learning systems natural vulnerability … “ -> awkward

- “Too constrained optimization in Huang et al. (2021) …” -> Informal

- In eq (6) and Algorithm 1, do we use all the data from the current target data? I think we should sample only a few of the current targets. If we sample, then what is the buffer size?

- In Algorithm 1, what does it mean by initializing D_T? D_T is data as shown in Fig. 1.

- “[0$\rightarrow$t[“ -> The right bracket is flipped.

- “However, as hinted while discussing Figure 2e earlier, this high stability is achieved at the expense of extremely low stability” -> at the expense of low plasticity?

- Fig 4 caption and the plot show inconsistent training, and test accuracy. Which one is training and which one is testing?

- “Such data points are the reason for the gap between the yellow and blue lines in Figure 4.” -> Fig 4 does not have yellow and blue lines.

There are some clarification questions for the authors.

Q1. Are all the backbones the same across all the methods compared in Tables 1 and 2? What are the UDA methods used for the proposed method? DANN [Ganin and Lempitsky, ICML 2015] or ADDA [Tzeng et al., CVPR 2017]? What are the UDA methods used for compared methods?

Q2. What is the buffer size used? Is it the same across all the compared methods in Tables and Figures?

Q3. In Table 2, why APA and AHA are not reported? The authors already claimed AHA as a stability metric relative to the ADiA, however, they do not report AHA in Table 2 without providing any reason.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has many errors and it lacks sufficient validation. Therefore, I would rate the quality and clarity low. The paper has a somewhat new idea of introducing specialist-generalist training for the task of CUDA. However, it is not thoroughly validated. Therefore, I would rate the originality somewhat high.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the authors propose a somewhat new idea of specialist-generalist training for the task of CUDA. The proposed method shows good performance compared to the existing method. However, the comparisons are unfair, and there are many unsupported claims. In addition, the presentation quality is quite unprofessional. Therefore, I would recommend a borderline reject.




======= post rebuttal update =======
Thanks for the responses from the authors. I understand that only the generalist is needed during inference. I also appreciate the additional results from training the smaller model. However, the improvement compared to the baseline is not very significant given the strong claims made by the authors. Also, I agree with Reviewer WdtT's point that the proposed method requires double memory compared to the baseline. To summarize, I am not convinced by the response. Therefore, I would recommend a reject.

content.comment:
**Reviewer Comment:** 
*" The proposed method uses two models which means there are twice the learnable parameters compared to the existing methods. Therefore, the comparisons with existing methods are unfair. To be fair, compared methods should learn the same amount of parameters. That means the compared method could expand the model along the way of continual learning. To justify the proposed method, there should be a baseline that expands learned parameters during each continual learning step, and finally, the total number of learned parameters is the same as the number of learned parameters of the proposed method. For now, we do not know if the good trade-off shown in the results is due to more parameters or due to the specialist-generalist learning paradigm."* 

**Response:** 
* We would like to draw the reviewer's attention to the fact that only the generalist is needed during inference.  The specialist is needed only to train the generalist and is not used during the inference phase. Moreover, these trained parameters are accessed sequentially during training, where the new parameters delete the older ones. 
* Regarding computational requirements, F2L (1) converges in fewer total number epochs, and (2) the number of optimizer update steps (i.e., number of gradient calculations) per epoch is less.

For the first point, training the F2L (i.e., both Generalist and Specialist) took 72% fewer epochs to converge than Bobu. This faster convergence is due to the simpler, non-conflicting, single objective function used for each stage of F2L.

For the second point, only the source and current target domain data are needed when training the specialist, which accounts for 76% of the training time in the F2Lapproach. Accordingly, 76% of the time, there is no need to feed forward/backward the samples from the memory buffer to calculate the loss/gradient of Eq.1. Accordingly, for the same batch size, a single epoch will involve fewer gradient calculations, and update steps. Note that for Bobu and other methods, all data in the memory buffer, source, and current target data must be processed during every optimizer step, see Eq.3. 

For Specialist, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source and current target data once
For Generalist, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source, current target, and memory buffer data once
For Bobu, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source, current target, and memory buffer data once 
* Although we showed that our proposed approach in its original form is at least computationally and memory equivalent to using a single encoder due to its simpler loss function, we did the following experiments to numerically demonstrate that F2L sustains its performance with limited number of parameters.  We trained a modified encoder architecture for both the generalist and specialist with only half the number of filters in the original LeNet-5 architecture. This effectively makes the total number of learned parameters the same. The table below still shows that F2L maintains its superiority even when a smaller architecture is used.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to address the problem of continuous unsupervised domain adaptation, with its main idea stems from the argument that simultaneously having the objective of domain alignment (related to plasticity) and the objective of knowledge retention (related to stability) in a single model would lead to the stability-plasticity dilemma, in which these two objectives could conflict each other thus leading to a trade-off between them as well as suboptimal model performance. In order to tackle the aforementioned issue, the authors explicitly use two networks respectively as domain specialist (i.e. acquiring new knowledge) and generalist (i.e. continuously learning and accumulating knowledge from previous specialists), where the domain specialist uses typical domain adaptation technique of aligning feature distributions across source and target domains via adversarial learning to adapt the knowledge from supervised source to unsupervised target domain, while the generalist adopts the training pairs (i.e. input image and the pseudo-label estimated by the corresponding domain specialist) accumulated from previous domains to perform the knowledge distillation from all the previous domains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The high level idea of the paper is easy to capture.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is hard to follow as having lots of variables not well defined and overloaded all the time. For instance, the discrepancy $d$ in Eq.1 is not well defined; $C_0$ is used in Eq.2 of Sec. 2.1 but defined later in Sec. 2.2; the variable $D$ is used to present "discriminator" and "domain" at the same time (e.g. in Algo. 1), which is extremely confusing; $M^t$ and $M_t$ are used to present the same thing which should be unified; in Algo.1 "train $E^t_T$ using the discriminator discrepancy loss $d[E_0(x_0),\hat{E^t_T}(x^t_T)]$" the variable $\hat{E^t_T}$ should be corrected by $E^t_T$.
- Although using two explicit network in proposed method to model the domain specialist and generalist seems to be with certain benefits, it is innegligible to double the overall computational cost as well as the memory usage. The comparison with respect to other baselines then seems to be unfair.
- Currently the proposed method seems to have no limit on the buffer size to store the samples from previous domains, in which such setting is also quite impractical. The experimental settings should include the information on memory size and even provide the studies on having limited memory size.
- Missing citations and discussion on the closely related works, e.g. the papers which cite the important baseline Bobu et al. (2018) of this submission, to name a few: Kumar et al., Understanding Self-Training for Gradual Domain Adaptation, PMLR 2020; Liu et al., Learning to Adapt to Evolving Domains, NeurIPS 2020.
- The experiments are mostly based on relatively simple datasets (e.g. RotatedMNIST and 5Digits) thus the results are not persuasive enough, while in the aforementioned missing references or the related works discussed in the submission (e.g. Tang et al.(2021)) there are further datasets used, e.g. CIFAR10, CIFAR100, tinyImagenet, Evolving Vehicles, caltrain, in which these should be included for making the experiments more complete and extensive.
- In the last sentence of page. 8, the authors claimed that "generalist does not only copy all the knowledge of the specialist, but it can generate its own knowledge" in which such argument seems quite awkward (for instance in Fig.5, I think the generalist simply learns the representation that is more rotation-invariant instead of generating "new" knowledge).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Due to lots of issues in terms of mathematical expressions, the clarity and the reproducibility of this paper are problematic.
The novelty of this paper is also insignificant as it adopts more networks (doubling the computational cost and memory usage) to achieve slightly better results in comparison to baselines.
The quality is unsatisfactory as well due to having missing references, insufficient experiments, and impractical model settings (e.g. unlimited buffer size).
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the problematic mathematical expressions, insignificant novelty, missing reference, insufficient experiments, and impractical model settings (please refer to weaknesses for more details), I would suggest to reject this paper from ICLR2023.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: (Reviewer 1-1)
content.comment:
**Reviewer Comment:**
*"Although using two explicit network in proposed method to model the domain specialist and generalist seems to be with certain benefits, it is innegligible to double the overall computational cost as well as the memory usage. The comparison with respect to other baselines then seems to be unfair."*
 
**Response:**
* Regarding computational requirements, F2L (1) converges in fewer total number epochs, and (2) the number of optimizer update steps (i.e., number of gradient calculations) per epoch is less.

For the first point, training the F2L (i.e., both Generalist and Specialist) took 72% fewer epochs to converge than Bobu. This faster convergence is due to the simpler, non-conflicting, single objective function used for each stage of F2L.

For the second point, only the source and current target domain data are needed when training the specialist, which accounts for 76% of the training time in the F2Lapproach. Accordingly, 76% of the time, there is no need to feed forward/backward the samples from the memory buffer to calculate the loss/gradient of Eq.1. Accordingly, for the same batch size, a single epoch will involve fewer gradient calculations, and update steps. Note that for Bobu and other methods, all data in the memory buffer, source, and current target data must be processed during every optimizer step, see Eq.3. 

For Specialist, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source and current target data once
For Generalist, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source, current target, and memory buffer data once
For Bobu, 1 Epoch= Processing all the source, current target, and memory buffer data once 
* Regarding the memory required to store the trained model parameters, we only store the most recent version of the Generalist and Specialist. The generalist is needed for inference during test time, while the specialist is used to initialize the new specialist for the next adaptation step. This indeed doubles the memory needed for saving the trained parameters. Thanks to the reviewer's comment, we have updated our method so that we store only the parameters trained for the generalist. We do this by using the generalist, both inference and initialization. We observed no significant performance deterioration. 
* Regarding Memory requirement, for the buffer size, we always use the same buffer size in all of our comparisons for fairness.

content.title: Reviewer 1-2
content.comment:
* **Reviewer Comment:** 
 
*" Currently the proposed method seems to have no limit on the buffer size to store the samples from previous domains, in which such setting is also quite impractical. The experimental settings should include the information on memory size and even provide the studies on having limited memory size. "* 

**Response:** 
* We always use the same buffer size in all our comparisons with SOTA methods for fairness.  Also notice that, as in our response to the previous comment, we have made a change to the algorithm so that the memory requirement for storing model parameters should be halved. 
* To answer the reviewer's concern regarding performance with minimal memory, for Rotated MNIST, we randomly sampled 5000,2500,1250 and 500 samples per domain and compared our approach against Bobu. As shown below, it is evident that our approach maintains its superiority regardless of buffer size.

| Method | ADiA | APA | AHA | ALA |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Bobu: lambda= 0.1, M=500.0 | -0.17 | 0.93 | 0.76 | 0.76 |
| F2L Generalist, M=500.0   | -0.11 | 0.95 | 0.83 | 0.84 |
| Bobu: lambda= 0.1, M=1250.0 | -0.14 | 0.93 | 0.81 | 0.80 |
| F2L Generalist, M=1250.0   | -0.06 | 0.95 | 0.89 | 0.89 |
| Bobu: lambda= 0.1, M=2500.0 | -0.13 | 0.93 | 0.83 | 0.81 |
| F2L Generalist, M=2500.0   | -0.04 | 0.95 | 0.92 | 0.92 |
| Bobu: lambda= 0.1, M=5000.0 | -0.13 | 0.94 | 0.84 | 0.81 |
| F2L Generalist, M=5000.0   | -0.02 | 0.95 | 0.93 | 0.93 |

content.title: Reviewer 1-3
content.comment:
* **Reviewer Comment:** 
 
*" Missing citations and discussion on the closely related works, e.g. the papers which cite the important baseline Bobu et al. (2018) of this submission, to name a few: Kumar et al., Understanding Self-Training for Gradual Domain Adaptation, PMLR 2020; Liu et al., Learning to Adapt to Evolving Domains, NeurIPS 2020. "* 

**Response:** 

The two papers are related but still would not fall into the same category as our method, and therefore, we would not include their methods in the numerical comparison. Below we explain how their methods are different from ours:
* Kumar et al.' do not attempt to address the forgetting problem (i.e., knowledge retention) in CUDA. They investigate an interesting and fundamentally different approach for solving the CUDA problem solely based on pseudo-labeling. They use pseudo labels for adaptation, while we use pseudo labels for knowledge retention.
* Liu et al., unlike Bobu et al. and Tang et al., are not proposing a replay-based CUDA method. Comparing our approach to theirs would be unfair to them. On rotated MNIST data, they couldn't reach 50% accuracy, while ours achieved more than 90%. Their performance is reasonable, given that they are proposing a memory-free method. They also require access to some target data at the meta-training step. Thus, it is not suitable for fully online CUDA settings.

content.title: Reviewer 1-4
content.comment:
* **Reviewer Comment:** 
 
*" The experiments are mostly based on relatively simple datasets (e.g. RotatedMNIST and 5Digits) thus the results are not persuasive enough, while in the aforementioned missing references or the related works discussed in the submission (e.g. Tang et al.(2021)) there are further datasets used, e.g. CIFAR10, CIFAR100, tinyImagenet, Evolving Vehicles, caltrain, in which these should be included for making the experiments more complete and extensive."* 

**Response:** 
We chose these datasets for the sake of fair comparison with the SOTA methods, as these are the datasets used in the original studies.
* Tang et al.(2021) used 5 Digit, Office Caltech, and Domain Net. We have 2/3 in our experimentation section and appendix. 
* Bobu et al.(2018) used Rotated MNIST and Atari-RL control tasks. We have 1/2 in our experimentation section and appendix.

content.title: Reviewer 1-5
content.comment:
* **Reviewer Comment:** 

*" In the last sentence of page. 8, the authors claimed that "generalist does not only copy all the knowledge of the specialist, but it can generate its own knowledge" in which such argument seems quite awkward (for instance in Fig.5, I think the generalist simply learns the representation that is more rotation-invariant instead of generating "new" knowledge)."* 

**Response:** 
* We would like to draw the reviewer's attention to the fact that Figure 5 discusses the results from Digit 5 dataset, not the Rotated MNIST. Accordingly, "rotation-invariant" in the reviewer's comment is no longer relevant to this figure.

* We agree with the reviewer that the term "generating new knowledge" might be confusing; accordingly, we will rephrase the relevant part in the revised paper if accepted.

content.title: Rebuttal Version and End of Discussion Period
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for their time and revision. Since we are approaching the end of the discussion period, we would appreciate it if we could hear feedback from the reviewers on our responses and revised manuscript.

In the revised manuscript, we have added appendices A3 and A4 to address the reviewer's concerns regarding computational and memory requirements.
Also, we have made the mathematical notation more rigorous. Additionally, we have made general cleaning and clarifications to reflect our responses to the reviewer's questions.
